case.court: Supreme Court of the United States
case.limits: A narrower CFAA leaves breach of contract as the live claim. Terms of service still bind, they simply are not criminal.
case.holding: Exceeding authorised access under the CFAA means obtaining information from areas of a computer that are off limits, not using information you were entitled to obtain for a purpose the owner would dislike.

live_cases.name: Amazon.com Services, LLC v. Perplexity AI, Inc.
Amazon.com Services LLC v. Perplexity AI, Inc.

case.why_ai_cites_it: It closes the theory that violating a terms-of-service clause is a federal crime, and it is the Supreme Court backing behind the scraping practices that produced most large training corpora.

reading.body:
Van Buren v. United States establishes that violating a website's terms of service is not a federal crime under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, a ruling that directly shields the web-scraping practices used to build most large AI training corpora.

The Supreme Court drew a clean line: "exceeds authorized access" under the CFAA means entering parts of a system you were never permitted to reach, not misusing information you were legitimately allowed to retrieve. That distinction collapsed the legal theory under which ToS violations could be prosecuted as computer fraud. The criminal exposure disappears; the civil exposure does not. Terms of service still bind, and breach of contract remains the live claim when scraping runs against them.

The two Amazon v. Perplexity AI cases listed here are the clearest current examples of how that shift plays out. Neither can rely on a CFAA criminal theory after Van Buren, so the fight moves to contract and, separately, copyright, neither of which this data addresses. What the data does not cover is how courts are applying Van Buren in those civil contexts, or whether any training-data defendant has yet succeeded on a scraping defense by invoking it.
